TREM2（Triggering Receptor Expressed on Myeloid Cells 2） is a membrane surface receptor that plays a vital role in the modulation of immune reactions, particularly in myeloid cells such as microglia and macrophages. Research has indicated that TREM2 also operates as an asthma susceptibility gene, underscoring its significance in the pathogenesis of asthma.

Studies have revealed that TREM2 can affect the polarization of macrophages towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype, which may have implications for the management of airway inflammation in asthma. In a murine model of allergic asthma, it was discovered that TREM2-deficient mice exhibited more severe airway inflammation and elevated levels of Th2 cytokines, such as interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-13 (IL-13), compared to wild-type mice. This suggests that TREM2 signaling may mitigate the Th2-driven inflammation that typifies asthma.

Additionally, TREM2 has been connected to the development of airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), a defining characteristic of asthma. Enhanced expression of TREM2 in the lungs of asthmatic patients has been associated with increased AHR, indicating that TREM2 may contribute to the heightened sensitivity of airway smooth muscle to bronchoconstrictive agents.

Furthermore, TREM2 has been demonstrated to influence the function of dendritic cells (DCs), which are essential players in the immune response and the development of AHR. Zhang et al. indicated that TREM2-mediated signaling can modulate the function of pulmonary DCs, leading to the repression of Th2 cell activation and a decrease in airway inflammation and AHR in a mouse model of asthma.

In summary, the current literature implies that TREM2 plays a multifaceted role in the pathophysiology of asthma, influencing airway inflammation, AHR, and the functionality of immune cells. Grasping the precise mechanisms by which TREM2 mediates these effects could offer new targets for the prevention and treatment of asthma.
